records.wording: Marcionite readings adopted. (1) "Remember all that he spoke to you" (ὅσα, Tertullian "quae", Epiphanius ὅσα) for NA27 "how he told you" (ὡς); NA27: ὅσα D c sys.c; McionT,E; Roth: secure. (2) "He has been raised" without "He is not here, but". Epiphanius quotes "Why do you seek the Living One among the dead? He has been raised. Remember…" in one run. When he cites the verse in his own words he always writes "He is risen (ἀνέστη), he is not here" (elenchus 76; Pan. 56.2.8): here he writes Luke's ἠγέρθη, which he does not use himself, and no "he is not here". NA27 cites McionE for ἠγέρθη alone. Roth judges the omission unattested rather than absent; the citation habit is the basis for the departure. Tertullian has "to you… in Galilee" and Epiphanius "while he was still"; together they give NA27's wording.
records.western: D and the Old Latin lack the whole of 6a, "he is not here, but he has been raised" (a Western non-interpolation). This text had "he has been raised".

records.wording: NA27. Tertullian attests that Jesus asked as if he did not know ("etiam dissimulans"). 19b ("a prophet, powerful in deed and word before God and all the people") is not cited by either witness. Class of 19b: U? (METHOD §3). Tertullian works through the passage in order (4.43.3–5): he paraphrases 24:15–19a and quotes 24:21, "we thought that he was the redeemer of Israel", arguing that Jesus would not have let the learners hold an opinion of him that was false (4.43.4). The description of 19b would fit that argument, as the crowd's "a great prophet" does at 7:16 (4.18.3), but he had the stronger words of 24:21 and used them; his passing over 19b (and 24:20) is not the silence of a witness who needed the passage, so the U− test is not met. Epiphanius (sch. 77) does not touch 24:19–20. No witness reports the words missing, so they stay in the text (METHOD §5.3).

records.wording: Marcionite reading adopted (retroversion): "we thought" (ἐνομίζομεν, Tertullian "putabamus") for NA27 "we hoped" (ἠλπίζομεν). The Latin cannot render "hoped", and Tertullian builds 4.43.4–5 on what the learners "thought" (existimare, five times). ἐνομίζομεν is also the reading of the Arabic and Persian Diatessaron and Ambrosiaster (Roth, citing IGNTP). Roth rates the verb possible only; this is a departure. Tertullian's "redeemer of Israel" can render "the one about to redeem Israel" and is probably his own noun (Roth, citing Lukas); NA27 is printed. 21b is unattested.

Both witnesses lack "the prophets": Epiphanius states that the text had "that I spoke to you" in place of "that the prophets spoke", and Tertullian quotes "all that he spoke to you" (NA27: ἐλάλησεν… πρὸς ὑμᾶς McionT,A; -σα McionA,E). Epiphanius' own elenchus shows the difficulty of his first person: "if he had said 'I spoke to you', they would have recognized him from that word; how then were their eyes opened at the breaking of bread?" The Adamantius Dialogue (198,5–7) also has the first person, but in the orthodox speaker's words. Roth: the final element uncertain.

records.wording: NA27 without "handle me and see" and without "flesh and" (attested omissions, METHOD §5.3). "Flesh and": both witnesses quote "a spirit does not have bones" (Tertullian twice). Epiphanius, when he cites the verse himself, has "flesh and bones" (Ancor. 91.6; Pan. 64.64.7; 77.9.5, as quoted by Roth), and in his elenchus here says that the Saviour has "bones and flesh"; his scholion has only "bones". NA27 cites McionT,E for the omission. "Handle me and see": Tertullian's quotation runs on from "it is I myself" to "for a spirit"; he argues from this verse that the body was real ("what could be clearer about the truth of the body?") and speaks only of hands and feet offered "for inspection" (4.43.8). An invitation to touch would have been his strongest evidence. Epiphanius' quotation also lacks it, but he also skips "that I am he myself", so his evidence is weaker here. Roth rates both omissions "may not have been present"; the departure rests on the witnesses' arguments and citation habits. Tertullian also cites the verse without both elements in Carn. Chr. 5.9 (as quoted by Roth), so the shorter form may not have been confined to Marcion's text.

"Everything written about me in the law of Moses and the prophets and the psalms must be fulfilled… Then he opened their minds to understand the scriptures… Thus it is written, that the Christ should suffer and on the third day rise." Tertullian passes from the request for food (24:41; 4.43.8) to the sending to the nations (24:47; 4.43.9) and ends his book by claiming that he has shown Jesus to be the Christ of the prophets; these verses would have been his proof text. Epiphanius does not cite them either. Classed probably absent.

"Beginning from Jerusalem", which NA27 punctuates with 24:48, is unattested and not printed. 24:47 is the last attested verse (METHOD §10).
